Kurt Gödel. An Austrian-American logician and mathematician born in 1906 and died in 1978. His Incompleteness Theorems, published in 1931, revealed fundamental limits to formal systems and shattered the dream of a complete, consistent axiomatisation of all mathematics. Working in logic and set theory, he also proved the consistency of the continuum hypothesis with the axioms of set theory and contributed to relativity theory by discovering rotating universes consistent with Einstein's equations. His theorems reshaped mathematics and philosophy, showing that provability has intrinsic bounds.

Gödel's First Incompleteness Theorem states that any consistent formal system powerful enough to express arithmetic is incomplete. There exist true statements that cannot be proven within that system. Gödel's Second Incompleteness Theorem says a consistent system cannot prove its own consistency. This is a corollary of the first. Together, these theorems showed that Hilbert's dream—a complete, consistent, decidable axiomatisation of mathematics—is impossible.

In logic and set theory, Gödel proved the completeness of first-order logic. Every logically valid sentence is provable. He showed the continuum hypothesis, that no set exists larger than the natural numbers but smaller than the real numbers, is consistent with ZFC set theory. However, this does not mean it is provably true or false. Gödel invented Gödel numbering, encoding logical formulas as numbers so arguments about proofs become arithmetic propositions.

He also discovered the Gödel metric, a solution to Einstein's field equations describing a rotating universe with conceptually simple but strange causal properties.

Gödel's theorems hit the mathematical world like a thunderbolt. The nineteenth and early twentieth centuries had seen a dream take shape: reduce all of mathematics to logic, find the axioms, and prove everything from them. Hilbert's decision problem asked whether a procedure exists to determine if any statement is provable. Gödel and later Church and Turing answered: no. Mathematics is fundamentally incomplete and undecidable. Yet Gödel also proved the completeness of first-order logic, showing that within limits, mathematical logic is sound. His work reshaped the philosophy of mathematics.
